title: Profiling glycoproteins enriched by surface functionalised nanoparticles
projectDescription: Biologically relevant biofluids, such as plasma and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), present significant challenges for glycoproteomic analysis due to their complex protein composition and the wide dynamic range of protein abundances. Nanoparticle-based (NP) enrichment has previously shown promise in enhancing the detection of low-abundance proteins, yet the glycoproteome has been underexplored. In this study, we investigate the use of NP enrichment with glycopeptide enrichment, in the form of a mixed-mode anion exchange chromatography, to characterize N- and O-linked glycopeptides in human plasma and CSF. Using the Seer Proteograph XT platform, we demonstrate that NP enrichment significantly enhances the N-glycoproteome coverage, particularly in plasma, and increases the detection of low abundant N-glycopeptides. When combined with MAX enrichment, a further improvement in glycopeptide detection was observed. For the O-glycoproteome, NP enrichment alone outperformed NP+MAX, suggesting that MAX may favor N-glycopeptides. We also explored CSF, a biofluid of interest for biomarker discovery, and found that NP enrichment increased proteome depth, with notable identification of extracellular vesicle protein biomarkers. Overall, this study highlights the synergy of NP-based enrichment and glycopeptide enrichment for enhancing the glycoproteome coverage of human biofluids and provides a valuable framework for studying glycoproteins in complex biological samples.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Both plasma and CSF samples were processed with the Proteograph XT Assay. In brief, 240 μL from the 40 plasma samples and 240 μL from the 420 CSF samples were transferred to Seer Sample Tubes for processing with the Proteograph XT Assay kit (S55R1100). Proteins were quantitatively captured in nanoparticle (NP) associated protein coronas. Proteins were subsequently denatured, reduced, alkylated and subjected to proteolytic digestion (trypsin and LysC). Peptides were purified and yields were determined (Thermo Fisher Scientific, catalog #23290). Peptides were dried down overnight with a vacuum concentrator before further enrichment or LC-MS/MS analysis. Samples were enriched for glycopeptides using a mixed-mode anion exchange protocol adapted from Bermudez and Pitteri. Briefly, the dried down nanoparticle-enriched peptides were resuspended with 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) in 50% acetonitrile (ACN) and the Oasis MAX cartridges (Waters) were preconditioned with 1 mL each of 100% ACN, 100 mM triethylammonium acetate (TEAA) in water, 1% TFA in water, and 1% TFA in 95% ACN. A 1 mL aliquot of 1% TFA in 95% ACN was applied to each cartridge and the samples were put over the aliquot. The flow through was collected and then reloaded to the cartridge a second time. The cartridges were washed with 1 mL of 1% TFA in 95% ACN and then glycopeptides were eluted with 1 mL of 0.1% TFA in 50% ACN. The glycopeptide-enriched samples were dried via vacuum centrifugation and resuspended 0.1% formic acid for LC-MS/MS. Samples were analyzed on an Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid Mass Spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a Thermo EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific). First, samples were reconstituted in 0.1% FA and loaded onto the analytical column at max flow rate with a pressure limit of 700 barr. Using a 300 µL/min flow rate for all steps of the gradient during acquisition, the method started with 1 min of isocratic flow at 3% buffer B (80% ACN with 0.1% FA), and peptides were linearly eluted using a 70-minute gradient ranging from 3% buffer B to 42% buffer B on a 50 cm PepMap Neo C18 analytical column (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The gradient then increased to 95% B over 1 minute, and the column was washed for 8 minutes with 95% B for a total of 80 minutes of acquisition time. After acquisition, the column was equilibrated at 3% B. Precursors were ionized using an EasySpray ionization source (Thermo Fisher Scientific) held at +2.0 kV compared to ground, the ion transfer tube temperature was held at 275°C, and the RF lens was set to 60%. The instrument method used a survey MS scan with resolution of 60k at 200 m/z, a normalized AGC target of 100% (400,000 charges), a maximum injection time of 123 ms, and a scan range of 400-1800 m/z. Monoisotopic peptide filtering was enabled, dynamic exclusion was set at 60 seconds after 1 occurrence with a ±10 ppm window, a minimum intensity threshold of 50,000 was used, and charges 2-5 were selected for fragmentation. MS/MS scans were performed in a data-dependent fashion with a cycle time of 3 seconds. Precursors were isolated using a 1.6 m/z quadrupole isolation width and were measured in the Orbitrap with an MS2 resolution of 30k at 200 m/z. sceHCD-pd-RTLS-EThcD was performed with 20, 30, and 45% normalized collision energies, a scan range of 120-2000 m/z, a normalized AGC target set to 100% (50,000 charges), and a maximum injection time of 59 ms. sceHCD-pd-RTLS-EThcD methods used a product-dependent trigger filter, requiring the presence of four of the following oxonium ion m/z values within the top 20 most abundant ions in the sceHCD MS/MS spectrum and with a ±15 ppm tolerance: 126.055, 138.0549, 144.0655, 168.0654, 186.076, 204.0865, 274.0921, 290.087, 292.1027, 308.0976, 366.1395, 454.1561, 657.2349. If those conditions were met, EThcD scans were triggered with calibrated ETD ion-ion reaction parameters, a supplemental HCD activation of 25% normalized collision energy, a normalized AGC target set to 200% (100,000 charges), a scan range of 120-4000 m/z, and a maximum injection time of 123 ms.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw data were searched using FragPipe (v22.0) with either the glyco-N-HCD or glyco-O-pair workflow default settings. A FASTA file containing all proteins found from NP enrichment of human plasma was created from publicly available data and used as a database for the plasma samples with decoys added by FragPipe. A FASTA file containing all proteins found from the DIA-NN search results when analysing the proteomic fraction of CSF was used as a database for the CSF data. When using the glyco-N-HCD workflow, a fixed modification was set as carbamidomethyl on C [+57.02146 Da], and variable modifications were set as oxidation on M [+15.9949 Da] and protein N-terminal acetylation [+42.0106 Da]. The default settings for a glyco search were loaded for PTM-Shepherd and the ‘Human_N-glycans-medium-252’ database was loaded without any modifications. N-glycoPSMs were filtered to contain ‘N’ in the ‘Assigned Modifications’ column and a q value of less than 1%. When using the glyco-O-pair workflow, a fixed modification was set as carbamidomethyl on C [+57.02146 Da], and variable modifications were set as oxidation on M [+15.9949 Da] and protein N-terminal acetylation [+42.0106 Da]. The ‘Human_O_glycan_32’ database was loaded without any modifications and default settings were selected for O-pair search. O-glycoPSMs were filtered to contain ‘S’ and/or ‘T’ in the ‘Assigned Modifications column’, ‘False’ in the ‘Has N Glyc Sequon’ column, an O-pair Score greater than 0 and a Level 1 Confidence level. All DIA was analyzed using DIA-NN (version 1.9.2). An in-silico library consisting of the reviewed human proteome (downloaded 10-15-2024), including common contaminants, was used for the experiment-specific library generation. All library files were searched concurrently, with the maximum missed cleavages set to 2, carbamidomethylation set as fixed modification, and N-term methionine excision set as variable modification. Peptides were searched with a length range between 7 and 30 and a charge range between 2 and 5. The precursor m/z range was set to 390-1010, and the fragment ion m/z range to 100-2000. Double-pass mode and match between runs (MBR) were enabled. Proteins were inferred on the Gene level, and no shared spectra were allowed. The precursor false discovery rate (FDR) was set to 1%. The CSF sample files were analyzed with a few modifications to the library generation files. All CSF sample files were searched concurrently. The generated library was used instead of the human proteome and contaminants previously used. Additionally, the MBR run was enabled. The library Q value, global Q value, protein group Q value, and protein group library Q value were all filtered at 1% FDR. Only proteotypic peptides were included in calculating the number of identified proteins. Subsequent figures were created using R (version 4.4.0).
